IR.rationale: A rise in intermediate yields relative to the policy rate signals expected tightening or higher discount rates. That state tends to weigh on near-term equity returns.

B.rationale: Widening Baa spreads together with weak high-yield returns mark a credit-stress state. In that state risk premia rise and expected equity returns are higher.

V.rationale: High equity implied volatility carries a variance risk premium and predicts higher subsequent returns. The premium is cleanest when the fear is equity-specific rather than driven by oil shocks.

AP.rationale: Weekly market returns show short-horizon reversal from liquidity provision and overreaction. A strong recent market week therefore tilts subsequent returns down.

ST.rationale: Conservative-investment stocks outperforming signals a defensive, risk-averse market tilt. Such tilts tend to precede compensation through higher market returns.

FX.rationale: The Australian dollar is a global risk-appetite and growth barometer. Its strength flags risk-on positioning that is partly priced in.

COM.rationale: Oil price changes carry information on global demand versus supply shocks. Markets are slow to impound this, so it bears on equity returns.

MC.rationale: Tight financial conditions reflect a constrained intermediary sector and elevated funding costs. Both affect equity returns over the following weeks.

ENDG.rationale: A high recent index return relative to its own history captures short-horizon reversal in index returns.

IR.rationale: Curve flattening reflects growth worries or policy tightening. Both raise future equity uncertainty, so steepening versus flattening informs volatility.

B.rationale: Deteriorating credit, with falling high-yield prices and widening spreads, raises leverage and default risk. That transmits into higher equity variance.

V.rationale: Implied volatility is forward-looking. It contains information on future realised variance beyond what past realised variance already shows.

AP.rationale: The leverage effect and volatility feedback mean negative market returns predict higher future variance.

ST.rationale: Quality outperforming while reversal strategies lose marks a flight to quality with impaired liquidity provision. That is a precursor of turbulent markets.

FX.rationale: Yen strength alongside broad dollar strength is a classic safe-haven, risk-off funding pattern. This pattern is associated with rising equity volatility.

COM.rationale: Falling broad commodity prices signal weakening global demand and deflationary pressure. Both raise uncertainty about earnings and future variance.

MC.rationale: Tight financial conditions combined with falling inflation expectations describe a deflationary stress state. That state is typically followed by elevated equity volatility.

ENDG.rationale: Realised variance mean-reverts, so a high recent variance relative to history shapes next-period variance beyond simple persistence.

IR.rationale: Abrupt term-spread moves reflect shifts in growth and policy expectations. These shifts change the odds of a sharp equity drawdown.

B.rationale: Credit markets often lead equities in pricing default risk. A credit-stress state raises the probability of equity crashes.

V.rationale: Elevated implied volatility across equity and oil widens the return distribution. That raises the probability of left-tail outcomes.

AP.rationale: Small caps underperforming signals tightening liquidity and risk aversion. This tends to precede broad market sell-offs.

ST.rationale: Losses on reversal strategies indicate liquidity providers are withdrawing. That makes cascading price declines more likely.

FX.rationale: Yen appreciation reflects carry-trade unwinding and safe-haven demand. These are associated with equity tail losses.

COM.rationale: Falling oil prices can signal collapsing global demand and stress in energy credit. Both raise downside tail risk for equities.

MC.rationale: Joint tight financial conditions and high measured financial stress identify a fragile system. In such a system large equity losses are more likely.

ENDG.rationale: Weak recent index returns reflect volatility clustering and downside momentum. That state raises the chance of another left-tail outcome.

IR.rationale: Falling intermediate yields relative to the policy rate signal expected easing. Expected easing often sets up sharp equity rebounds.

B.rationale: After credit stress, risk premia are elevated. Relief can produce outsized equity gains.

V.rationale: High implied volatility widens the distribution on both sides. It also embeds a large risk premium, raising the odds of right-tail rebounds.

AP.rationale: Sharp market declines are frequently followed by large reversals as liquidity returns and risk premia compress.

ST.rationale: A flight-to-quality, liquidity-strained state precedes high-dispersion periods. Such periods contain the largest rebound weeks.

FX.rationale: Yen safe-haven appreciation marks risk-off episodes. Those episodes are often followed by strong relief rallies.

COM.rationale: Commodity sell-offs coincide with global demand scares. These scares tend to reverse, along with equities, producing large gains.

MC.rationale: High financial stress raises volatility and expected risk premia. That increases the likelihood of large upside moves when stress eases.

ENDG.rationale: Weak recent index returns set up mean-reverting rebounds and sit in high-volatility regimes. Both raise the right-tail probability.
